catalog_quote: Stress. A stressed syllable is indicated by an acute sign over ... vowel. Primary stress is always on either the ultima or the penult: paraʔuliʔán 'home.' Secondary stress is indicated only when it is peculiar to a constituent prefix: nágpakayámu 'too much, too many.' ... Other things being equal, stressed forms precede unstressed forms and independent words precede elements marked with a +. Where two identical forms differ only in meaning, the order followed should be taken as indicative of their relative frequency in current Hanunóo speech. If a Hanunóo form is repeated (separated by a comma) with the only difference being that of stress, the first stress pattern is to be considered the more frequent and will usually be the only one used in the derivatives that follow. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim on Conklin 1953 printed p.5-6 (held page scan and scanned pg-009/); the record's ellipsis matches a print defect in the scan. (2) Deciding source is a dictionary phonetic key (1953) by the principal Hanunóo fieldworker; Glottolog lists no grammar/phonology for the language, and the one later descriptive work (Epo 2014, held) just cites Conklin 1953:5 and adds a stress-shift minimal pair (la'wud vs lawud', Table 4 p.13), so Conklin is the best available and is. sources.quote: Precursor of Zorc 1993 with the same wording: Hanunoo listed among languages from which contrastive word-accent examples 'could also be drawn' (p.1) and among languages with inherited length (p.2).

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David. 1978. Proto-Philippine word accent: innovation or Proto-Hesperonesian retention? In S.A. Wurm & Lois Carrington (eds.), Second International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics: Proceedings, Fascicle 1, 67-119. Pacific Linguistics C-61. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: p.70: study 'limited to only the penultimate and ultimate syllables of full words'. p.71 Table 1, Group A (languages with contrastive accent realised as penult length + pitch/stress) includes 'Han ba:gaq 'lungs' / bagaq 'swelling, lump''; following text: 'vowel length (or shortness) is clearly the most predominant feature at the word level. Stress is usually predictable (depending on the length or shortness of the penult vowel)'. Independent Hanunóo minimal pair from a linguist with his own Hanunóo field notes (zorc.net).
sources.locator: printed p.70-71, sec. 2.1 and Table 1 'Accent as Realised in some Philippine Languages', Group A
